originalTitle: Laika has spent 20 years building up to Wildwood

content: Across several decades in Hollywood, Caleb Deschanel has seen a lot. He served as cinematographer on films like The Passion of the Christ and The Patriot, worked on sequences in The Godfather and Titanic, and directed a few episodes of Twin Peaks. Even still, nothing could quite prepare him for his first stop-motion project: working as the cinematographer on Wildwood, the latest release from Coraline studio Laika. While he knew that stop-motion was a long and involved process, he was still surprised by just how much work went into these movies. “When I started I thought it was one thing, and then I quickly found out that it was another thing,” Deschanel says. “It was much more complicated than I expected.” Wildwood has been a long time coming. Laika CEO Travis Knight originally optioned the rights for the book of the same name, written by Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, in 2011. But production didn’t begin until a decade later. “I’ve been working on it in some form or another for 16 years,” Knight, who also directed Wildwood, says. “The reason why I stuck with it, the reason why I had to make this movie no matter what, is because of what it meant to me personally. Underneath it all, it’s a story about love and loss and grief, it’s about the impossible things that love asks of us, and that meant something to me personally in a very profound way.” It’s also the biggest production Laika has ever undertaken. Wildwood tells the story of a young girl named Prue who has to venture into the “impassable wilderness” that surrounds Portland in order to find her baby brother. When she enters the forest she discovers a fantasy realm reminiscent of Narnia, with magical spells, talking animals, and warring factions. It required nearly 50 animators and more than 200 puppets to pull it off, and the film is full of ambitious sequences, like a 12-minute battle with dozens of soldiers and a chase scene through a bustling Portland, where Prue’s brother is carried away by a gigantic murder of crows. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/26848892-9741-11f1-ad63-72f37b66ec04_wwd.bts_.00083.rgb_.approved-copy.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/f9a99bb0-9744-11f1-a125-ce84cd5b2caf_wwd.bts_.00326.rgb_.approved-copy.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] According to head of animation Brad Schiff, the studio’s ethos involves mixing “old-school craft with modern technology.” With each project, he says, Laika develops new techniques. If something works well, they then push the idea even further on the next project. For instance, on Laika’s previous film, Missing Link, the main character was outfitted with a diaphragm so that when an animator turned a screw on the puppet’s back, the diaphragm could expand or contract, creating the illusion that it was breathing. This has since become the standard for puppets in Laika’s films. These may sound like small details, but over the years they add up. For costume designer Deb Cook, there wasn’t a single innovation on Wildwood that stood out to her, but rather the sheer number of tools she had at her disposal. “Over time we’ve gathered together a library of techniques that we’ve been able to put into practice on this movie,” she says. This was especially important on Wildwood, which features a huge range of costumes; in the city sequences everyone is dressed in modern clothing, whereas in the forest characters have more fantastical looks. For Wildwood, many of the advancements came down to materials. The costumes made use of more flexible fabrics, for example, and the team also engineered a new process for creating silicone that’s lighter and more durable than what they previously used. “We’ve done this so we can wean ourselves off of foam latex, which is stinky and it shrinks over time, and five years later it kind of just crumbles,” says Oliver Jones, head of characters and practical effects. “There are advantages to rethinking a lot of these materials that were our go-to probably since King Kong.” The scale of Wildwood has also forced the studio to adopt another seemingly much more boring practice: being better organized. “They’ve been misplaced,” Cook says, when asked if she’s ever lost a puppet. “There’s now a very sophisticated tracking system because there are so many moving parts, and so many stages around the studio.” And while much has been said about the large and elaborate sequences in the film — Knight says the epic battle scene is “probably the most technically challenging thing that we’ve ever done” — all of these techniques are designed to imbue more humanity into characters that are portrayed by puppets. In that regard, small details like the flow of fabric or the impression of breathing are vitally important. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/2f80b4c0-9741-11f1-9111-de501831d785_wwd.bts_.00093.rgb_.approved-copy.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/1acddd60-9745-11f1-99f0-f61ab3b9ac56_wwd.bts_.00350.rgb_.approved-copy.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “We also have really subtle and intimate scenes, quiet scenes that don’t have a lot of flash, that have virtually no sound design or music, where the only thing that you’re experiencing is the grief of a father talking about a secret that he’s been holding on to for 15 years, or a quiet moment of a woman grieving the loss of her son,” Knight explains. “These are moments where you have nowhere to hide and the performances of these little puppets — these little assemblages of steel and silicon and fabric that have no life of their own — completely spring to life because of the hand and the artistry of the human behind it. Those are the moments that I’m most proud of.” In this way, the long road to Wildwood hitting theaters makes a lot of sense. chineseContent: 在好莱坞的几十年里，凯莱布·丹斯切尔 (Caleb Deschanel) 见识了很多。他在《基督受难记》和《爱国者》等电影中担任电影摄影师，参与了《教父》和《泰坦尼克号》的拍摄，并执导了《双峰》的几集。即便如此，他还是没有为他的第一个定格动画项目做好准备：在 Coraline 工作室 Laika 的最新作品《怀尔德伍德》中担任摄影师。虽然他知道定格动画是一个漫长而复杂的过程，但他仍然对这些电影投入的工作量感到惊讶。 “当我开始时，我以为这是一回事，然后我很快发现这是另一回事，”丹斯切尔说。 “这比我想象的要复杂得多。”怀尔德伍德已经等了很长时间了。 Laika 首席执行官特拉维斯·奈特 (Travis Knight) 最初于 2011 年购买了由 Decemberists 主唱科林·梅洛伊 (Colin Meloy) 撰写的同名书籍的版权。但直到十年后才开始制作。 “我已经以某种形式致力于这部电影 16 年了，”同时执导过《怀尔德伍德》的奈特说道。 “我之所以坚持下去，为什么我无论如何都要拍这部电影，是因为它对我个人来说意味着什么。在这一切的背后，这是一个关于爱、失落和悲伤的故事，它是关于爱对我们提出的不可能的事情，这对我个人来说意义重大。”这也是莱卡有史以来最大的制作。 《怀尔德伍德》讲述了一个名叫普鲁的小女孩的故事，她必须冒险进入波特兰周围“无法通行的荒野”才能找到她的小弟弟。当她进入森林时，她发现了一个让人想起纳尼亚的奇幻王国，那里有魔法咒语、会说话的动物和交战的派系。需要近50名动画师和200多个木偶来拉动
